and needless suffering while opening the gates to a flood of garbage.

be nothing stopping the industry from being driven straight into the garbage with cheap junk. People will learn the difference when they are
tired with junk. They will look elsewhere. This isn't an investment in America's future; it's a death sentence.

General Comment
1: It's nonfunctional without theft
This new technology requires huge amounts of data to do what it does, to supposedly teach computers how to “draw” and “write” and
“talk” like people, and that data isn't coming from nowhere. It's coming from all the information that's currently accessible online, including
encyclopedias, periodicals and media broadcast websites, art community image libraries, creative writing online libraries, public record
archives and any picture, published story, or social media post shared onlin. What this means, in short, is: if you have ANY sort of
footprint of existence online, it's currently up for grabs for a tech company to use to teach their generators how to “make things.” And no
one will be compensated for it.
On top of all this? It's not even actually Artificially Intelligent. “AI” is a sci-fi buzzword covering up the fact that these programs are merely
extremely complicated average generators, without any real “cognition” or “understanding” behind them. They are the equivalent of a
trained pigeon, which receives seeds when it pecks the word “FOOD” on a screen: it does not know “how to read”, it does not
understand that the word “FOOD” means anything edible, it has merely been conditioned to expect a result when it interacts with a
particular shape of letters. They cannot, and will not ever understand the full breadth of meaningfulness of communication that comes from
real human beings and what they produce.
2: It's Horrible for the Environment
The development phase of GPT-4, the currently most advanced Large Language Model Text Generator to date, put electricity supply
demands on power plants that created carbon emissions output equivalent to powering over 1,300 homes for a year. And when it's
working to process inputs, it produces more, with GPT-3's daily usage profile producing 8.4 tons of CO2 annually. And all those data
centers need water to cool. According to the Washington Post in collaboration with the University of California, Riverside, if 1 in 10
Americans used ChatGPT weekly for a year, it would require the amount of water equal to that used by the entirety of Rhode Island for
1.5 days. And whether you like it or not, the anthropogenic impact of human industrial activity on the environment is a known and proven
scientific fact. Waking up and seeing news briefs of the city of Los Angeles literally looking like the gateway to Hell should be illustrative
enough of the dire consequences of neglecting to manage water consumption.
3: It Devalues the Essential Human Expression of Creativity
No matter what your philosophical definition of “meaningful art” is, it is an activity that has intrinsic value because it's something that only
human beings do. But what “AI” algorithmic generation does is say that the only art that means anything or has any value is the art that
“looks good enough” to be a product. There is no space in AI Algorithmic Generated art for abstraction, impressionism, stylization and
any of the innumerable ways that the human mind looks at the world, and attempts to outwardly express the act of interpreting it. For AI,
there is only the pre-existing library of images, and what is most frequently occurring to draw from.
There was a study recently that attempted to prove that the average layperson “likes AI art” because it manages to reach the same level of
a mediocrity as mundane consumer decoration, and the average person is too stupid to know what “critically worthy” art is anyways. But
not only is that insulting of every person's ability to appreciate the many different kinds of art, it's also a screen for a deeper, more serious
issue. The issue at stake in the implementation of AI is not only “what art is good enough to be consumed” but rather “do humans deserve
to do art at all, or should it be handed over to mechanization?” If a computer algorithm can generate an image that is good enough for
business purposes, there’s no reason for a human to make a painting. Why should a person spend time writing story if a machine can do it

faster and cheaper? Every action that can be done sufficiently by automation MUST be turned over entirely to automation to do. Every
human activity must be proven to have some kind of quantifiable value, and if it does not measure up, something more “productive” must
be done instead. If a computer can make the art, write the story, or film the movie for free, then all the painters, writers, poets, cartoonists,
actors, filmmakers, and everyone else must do something else worthy of pay
It is with these points in mind that I insist that US regulation treats "AI" as the dangerous, wasteful novelty that it truly is.

* AI is overhyped and is fleecing the eyes of the American public.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
Email: 
General Comment
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

using information expressly given to it by contributors. This training must be rigorous to avoid errors; sometimes taking months or years of
development and rigorous testing. Recent events with software technology, such as the 2024 CrowdStrike Incident serves as a grim
reminder of what can happen when even seemingly dependable systems have a critical issue. The AI technology must ensure that factual

for previous established uses of Intellectual Property and Copyright law. Many Americans, both individual and as parts of Corporations,
rely on Intellectual Property and Copyright law to protect their intellectual investments. Any AI Action Plan that is developed in this
country needs to ensure that carte blanche is not given to any AI developer that would infringe on the rights of practically every American
for its own benefit. If Intellectual Property and Copyright law is weakened any way by this action plan, that will cause severe IP issues and
set off years of legal strife in many Intellectual fields such as Art, Music, Motion Pictures, Interactive Entertainment, and this would reach

into information that it does not intellectually own. The Copyright Office recently has stated as a part of their policy that it must uphold the

many Americans that have benefited this country through their creative efforts. I strongly urge the policymakers that read this to consider

development.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an attorney and writer who recently started a small publishing company. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and 
knowledge to build my business. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small 
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of 
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our 
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing 
American creators’ copyrighted work legal, despite clear legal precedent that says it is not. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests 
and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim 
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the 
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music 
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living 
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech 
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair 
marketplace with competition:
* First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and 
where our work is used by AI systems.

* Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, and the primary value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators,
not Big Tech.
* Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
If AI companies are allowed to simply steal copyrighted works, it will result in a dearth of new creative works produced by humans, so
that the only thing left for the AI to be trained on is itself. This digital inbreeding will in turn make the AI models themselves worse - just
look at the genetics of the British Royal Family. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

games, and while it hasn't yet had much of an impact on comics it feels like it will only be a matter of time. I do not think the things AI can
create will ever be very good, but I do worry that the draw of not having to pay someone for their work will be irresistible. We could end
up in a situation where the next generation of artists (or, to bring up another field, the next generation of coders) never get the opportunity
to develop their skills. We could lose our culture to a flood of averaged images, bland text, and incomprehensible software if we're not
careful.

can replace humans, if that's ever desirable. We should be very careful about how much power we give a statistical model over the art we
interact with and the software we use every day.

allow them to steal any piece of written work in their quixotic quest for a machine that wishes to kill everyone who didn’t help it be born is

General Comment
I am writing to ask that the government deny OpenAI the ability to train on copyrighted material.
I don’t understand why decades of copyright law are suddenly out the window just because one company claims that they can’t deliver on
their goals unless they’re able to violate it. If OpenAI as a company is unable to deliver on its goals, on their own terms, then why should
they be given extra help to succeed? Is this really aligned with our country’s great history of industry? The core of the American dream is
that you’re able to make your own way, on your own terms. This is also essential to the spirit of capitalism. But now, again, here is a
company like OpenAI claiming that they’re incapable of developing an effective product, unless they’re able to steal from copyrighted
works. This makes no sense to me.
Why can’t they source from public works, that have moved out of copyright domain? Why is this brand new industry, which has yet to
prove itself, allowed to skirt laws and norms that have applied through copyright law? Can’t we at least put laws into place first, where
creators can sign an agreement for their works to be used for AI training? Wouldn’t it make sense to allow a creator to benefit from their
own work, in the same way that movie studios must sign contracts first, before moving forward with an adaptation/production.
I think it’s premature, and that OpenAI is overstepping as a company. I think if the government permits this, they open themselves up to
additional lawsuits, which could be avoided if they were willing to work with creators first, rather than taking directions from a single
company. I will also add that a recent case, Reuters vs. Ross Intelligence, ruled against AI’s access to copyright law. There is also
currently an ongoing case with Meta. With these as established precedent, I can’t see how this doesn’t lead to further litigation, and a huge
waste of government time and resources while trying to decide on a request that has already been cemented via copyright law.
Please deny OpenAI’s request to train on copyrighted material. Please consider the implications of this sort of request, and the amount of

March 15, 2025
From:
Cody Tibbs
Enterprise Engineer
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies,
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment

White House AI Action Plan Comment Letter

March 15, 2025 
From: 
Hojin Jung 
Character Designer & 2D Animator 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who makes my living as an artist in the entertainment industry- 
specifically animation. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my resume, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living. I have been thinking about 
going freelance and operating as a small business with my artwork and skills as well. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to 
create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies,
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment, marketing, and publishing
industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a
decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where

our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology but I do take a stand against the wholesale theft of American creativity. We should not sacrifice the hard work of
hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
March 14, 2025
From:
Michelle Johnson
Teacher and hobby artist

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition… require transparency… disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

General Comment
The term "AI", as its currently used, is little more than a search engine. The training data is fed into a large probabilistic model that free
associates words together.
These tools have little, if any, value. They frequently "hallucinate" due to their probabilistic design. They have no notion of truth or
accuracy. Their only value is to create a list of words that approximate a sentence to the reader.
That said, what they're good at is regurgitating the input that they receive. This input is the real contributions of human effort. The
allowance of fair use to their training on copyrighted material is an affront to the human effort used to create what they receive.
Furthermore, what we're seeing in the market has the classic signatures of a speculative bubble. The "AI war" is nothing more than a
competition between the hucksters vying for supremacy in the eyes of the investors. The only way to win is not to play the game.
I do not support changing copyright law to favor AI use. And I do not support assigning copyright protection to the output of AI models.
This is a flawed business that shouldn't be allowed to exist.

PUBLIC SUBMISSION

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan
Document: NSF_FRDOC_0001-DRAFT-4019
Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Robert Iadicicco
General Comment
I am an everyday American who makes art professionally.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American livelihoods
like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI-RFI-2025-4019.rationale: The commenter argues that AI training uses creators’ copyrighted work without consent or compensation and opposes creating copyright exemptions, directly matching the copyright/IP concern. The submitter identifies as an individual (“everyday American”) and does not represent an organization.

hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems. This consent should always be given via opt-in settings, not opt-out that assumes people want to
participate. Opt-out settings are predatory and abusive.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) networks poses a significant threat to the climate of our planet and, consequently, to the
continued survival of the human race. While AI has the potential to drive innovation and efficiency, its environmental costs are often
overlooked, leading to dire consequences for our ecosystems and future generations.
Firstly, the energy consumption associated with training and operating AI models is staggering. Large-scale AI systems require vast
amounts of computational power, which translates into substantial electricity usage. According to recent studies, training a single AI model
can emit as much carbon as the lifetime emissions of several cars. As the demand for AI technologies grows, so too does the energy
required to support them, often sourced from fossil fuels. This exacerbates greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to climate change and
its associated impacts, such as extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and biodiversity loss.
Moreover, the infrastructure needed to support AI networks—data centers, cooling systems, and extensive server farms—further strains
our planet's resources. These facilities not only consume enormous amounts of energy but also require significant water resources for
cooling, leading to water scarcity in regions already facing environmental stress. The environmental footprint of AI extends beyond energy
consumption; it also encompasses the extraction of rare minerals and metals necessary for hardware production, which often involves
environmentally destructive mining practices.
Additionally, the deployment of AI in various sectors, such as agriculture and manufacturing, can lead to unsustainable practices that harm
the environment. For instance, AI-driven precision agriculture may optimize resource use, but it can also encourage over-reliance on
chemical fertilizers and pesticides, further degrading soil health and water quality. The automation of industries can lead to increased
production rates, which, without proper regulation by a governing body, can result in overconsumption and waste, further straining our
planet's ecosystems.
Finally, the societal implications of AI's environmental impact cannot be ignored. As climate change accelerates, vulnerable populations—
often those least responsible for emissions—will bear the brunt of its effects especially in areas already often battered by severe weather
events. The displacement of communities, loss of livelihoods, and increased competition for dwindling resources could lead to social unrest
and conflict, and a total collapse of the current United States of America as we have come to know it as its citizens.
In conclusion, while artificial intelligence networks offer numerous benefits, their harmful impact on the climate and the potential threat to
human survival must be critically examined. It is imperative that we prioritize sustainable practices in the development and deployment of
AI technologies, ensuring that they contribute positively to our planet rather than exacerbate the environmental crises we face. Without a
concerted effort to mitigate these risks, we may find ourselves jeopardizing not only the health of our planet but also the future of humanity
itself.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.

If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.

marketplace with competition:

our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.

training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Justin Morris 
General Comment
I am an artist, writer, and translator. My creative output and the copyrights to it that I own are fundamental to my ability to continue living.
My business and those of others in my fields have already been adversely affected by AI companies' unethical and illegal use of copyright-
protected intellectual property for the training of models whose explicit purpose is to replace human workers such as myself. AI absolutely
cannot be given carte blanche to steal the work of human creators and violate the sanctity of their copyright protections based on the
flimsy justification that the AI companies' business models cannot succeed without such widespread theft and violation.
We suffer no other industry to violate our rights in this way due to the financial burdens of their businesses, AI can be no exception. If their
model cannot succeed without theft and the abrogation of creators' rights to protect their work, then the only correct outcome must be
that the AI businesses fail. We exist in a capitalist system where market pressures dictate who succeeds and who fails. AI businesses have
done nothing to deserve exception from this, and the harm that they have already caused–to say nothing of the further harm that a
regulatory carveout sanctioning their intellectual property theft would do–has been palpably felt in my community.
Hold AI businesses to the same standard as all other individuals and businesses are held. Do not give them unfettered access to publicly
posted creative works normally subject to copyright protections. Let them bear the same burden to ethically and legally support their
business that all other Americans do. Basic fairness and the sanctity of the rule of law demands no less.

AI absolutely cannot be given carte blanche to steal the work of human creators and violate the sanctity of their copyright protections... Do not give them unfettered access to publicly posted creative works normally subject to copyright protections.
